items.title: Why Enterprise AI Isn't Delivering ROI | Ahmed Bashir, DevRev
items.summary: The pattern is familiar to every enterprise leader: the AI demo works perfectly, the enterprise deployment disappoints, and the CIO can't explain why. Ahmed Bashir, Chief Technology Officer of DevRev, joins Craig Smith with a specific and well-supported answer: the problem isn't the model. It's that enterprise data is organizationally complex, fragmented across dozens of tools, locked behind conditional permissions, organized by custom schemas, and every prominent AI benchmark tests models against flat files with pre-packaged data, which has nothing to do with how enterprise data actually lives. DevRev's Enterprise Bench is the first benchmark to test complete agent harnesses against a realistically distributed enterprise environment where the agent must find, relate, and validate information before performing any task, and the results expose a gap that pre-packaged benchmarks hide entirely. The most striking finding: DevRev's system achieves 50% higher accuracy than Claude Code using the identical Opus family model. The entire delta comes from the shared memory layer, the governance, semantic understanding, and orchestration that sits between the model and the enterprise data. Ahmed's analogy is precise: upgrading a CPU cannot compensate for insufficient RAM, because they perform fundamentally different functions. A more powerful model cannot make up for a weak memory layer for the same reason. The conversation also covers why Enterprise Bench aspires to be for AI agents what TPC benchmarks became for databases in the 1980s - the independent standard that ended vendor benchmark wars and gave buyers a genuinely apples-to-apples comparison - and why the build-vs-buy question in enterprise AI has a quantifiable answer for the first time, visible on a public leaderboard that puts DIY configurations directly alongside proprietary systems. items.title: Interview #103 Somya Kapoor, CEO of IFS Loops
items.summary: Somya Kapoor, CEO of IFS Loops, breaks down why most AI agent projects fail on change management rather than technology, and why a company that waits for perfect data will never get an agent deployed. She explains why building an agent is now easy enough for an 11-year-old while getting one into production is not, how an agent that starts at 40-50% accuracy can reach 80-85% in weeks with a human handling the exceptions, and why we demand perfection from machines when people are only about 70% productive at their jobs. Somya also dives into why every digital worker needs a supervisor agent keeping an audit trail, and who answers when an agent misprocesses a purchase order at 3 AM. Finally, she shares which jobs agents will take and which new ones they create, and why regulation, not technology, will keep a human signing off in industries where one outage can leave millions without power. items.title: Interview #102 Alex Salazar, Co-founder & CEO at Arcade.dev
items.summary: Alex Salazar, Co-founder & CEO at Arcade.dev, breaks down why treating AI agents as teammates is an architectural dead end, and why they should be treated as software that is unpredictable enough to count as adversarial. He explains why security is usually the first team to say no, why an agent's own permissions are only half the problem when an intern could ask it for the CEO's pay, and what has to be true before a bank lets an agent wire money, from payee accounts registered ahead of time to checking the CRM so a refund is not hallucinated. Alex also dives into approval fatigue, research showing people check an agent's work less when they see it as a peer, and why no model should ever be trusted, open-weight or not. Finally, he shares why the vendors behind most agent strategies likely did not exist before 2024, and why agents moving money will feel mundane by the end of next year. items.title: Why Stripe Cut 500,000 Internal Docs Down to 5,000?
items.summary: What happens when AI agents start relying on the same messy docs your team already struggles to search? Demetrios hops into a Waymo in San Francisco with Dave Nunez , founder and CEO of Falconer and co-author of Documentation for Developers. They talk about why developers and agents need different things from docs, why agents sometimes skip up-to-date instructions, and how a stale internal document can contribute to a production incident. Dave shares how Stripe cut roughly 500,000 internal docs down to 5,000 worth maintaining. The conversation also covers how to capture the reasoning behind engineering decisions, when a diagram beats a wall of text, and who owns the fallout when an agent acts on bad information.
